# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and a major cause of ischemic stroke, accounting for approximately 15–20% of all cardioembolic strokes [1]. The left atrial appendage (LAA) is the dominant source of thrombus formation in non-valvular AF, with autopsy and transesophageal echocardiographic studies demonstrating that more than 90% of atrial thrombi originate from this structure [2]. Oral anticoagulation (OAC), with either vitamin K antagonists or direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), remains the cornerstone of stroke prevention [3]. However, a substantial proportion of patients have contraindications to long-term anticoagulation, bleeding risk, or poor adherence [4]. Percutaneous LAA closure (LAAC) has emerged as a mechanical alternative to pharmacologic stroke prophylaxis [5].

## Rationale and Devices

The conceptual basis of LAAC is the exclusion of the appendage from systemic circulation, thereby eliminating the predominant nidus for thromboembolism [2]. Several devices have been developed, broadly categorized into endocardial occluders and epicardial ligation systems [6]. The Watchman device (Boston Scientific) is the most extensively studied endocardial implant, followed by its iteration, the Watchman FLX [7]. The Amplatzer Cardiac Plug and its successor, the Amulet (Abbott), employ a dual lobe-and-disc design [8]. Epicardial approaches, such as the LARIAT suture-delivery system, achieve appendage ligation through a combined endocardial-epicardial technique [9].

## Evidence from Randomized Trials

The PROTECT AF trial was the first randomized study to compare the Watchman device with warfarin in patients with non-valvular AF, demonstrating non-inferiority for the composite endpoint of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death [10]. The subsequent PREVAIL trial addressed early procedural safety concerns but did not meet one of its prespecified efficacy endpoints [11]. Pooled analyses of PROTECT AF and PREVAIL, with five-year follow-up, confirmed comparable stroke prevention and suggested reductions in hemorrhagic stroke, cardiovascular mortality, and bleeding [12,13]. The PRAGUE-17 trial extended evidence by comparing LAAC with DOACs in high-risk patients, demonstrating non-inferiority [14]. The Amulet IDE trial established non-inferiority of the Amulet device relative to the Watchman for safety and effectiveness [15].

## Registries and Real-World Data

Large registries have complemented randomized data. The EWOLUTION registry reported high implant success and low procedural complication rates in real-world practice [16]. The U.S. National Cardiovascular Data Registry LAAO Registry, encompassing tens of thousands of procedures, documented procedural success exceeding 95% with declining complication rates as operator experience increased [17]. Observational comparisons have suggested favorable outcomes versus anticoagulation in selected populations [18].

## Procedural Considerations and Imaging

Procedural success depends on detailed preprocedural imaging to assess LAA anatomy, which exhibits considerable morphologic variability ("chicken wing," "windsock," "cactus," and "cauliflower" types) [19]. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) remains the standard for procedural guidance and device sizing, although cardiac computed tomography is increasingly used for planning [20]. Intracardiac echocardiography offers an alternative for guidance, reducing the need for general anesthesia [21]. Transseptal puncture in an inferior and posterior position facilitates coaxial device deployment [22].

## Complications and Device-Related Thrombus

Procedural complications include pericardial effusion, device embolization, and vascular access events, though rates have declined with improved technique [17]. Peri-device leak following implantation is common but its clinical significance remains debated [23]. Device-related thrombus (DRT) occurs in approximately 3–4% of patients and is associated with increased thromboembolic risk [24]. Identifying predictors of DRT, including deep implantation and hypercoagulable states, is an active area of investigation [25].

## Antithrombotic Management

Optimal post-implant antithrombotic regimens remain uncertain. Initial protocols used short-term warfarin followed by dual antiplatelet therapy [10], while contemporary practice often employs DOAC-based or single/dual antiplatelet strategies, particularly in patients with bleeding contraindications [26]. The ASAP study demonstrated feasibility of LAAC in patients ineligible for anticoagulation using antiplatelet therapy alone [27].

## Guidelines and Future Directions

Current guidelines assign LAAC a role in patients with contraindications to long-term anticoagulation, typically as a class IIb recommendation [3,28]. Ongoing randomized trials, including CHAMPION-AF and CATALYST, are comparing LAAC directly with DOACs in broader populations and may expand indications [29]. Combined procedures, such as concomitant LAAC with catheter ablation or structural interventions, and refinements in device design continue to evolve [30].

## Conclusion

Percutaneous LAAC provides an effective mechanical alternative for stroke prevention in AF patients unsuitable for long-term anticoagulation. Robust randomized and registry data support its safety and efficacy, though questions regarding optimal patient selection, antithrombotic management, and comparison with DOACs in lower-risk populations await resolution from ongoing trials.
